summary: An IAB statement of concern about voice traffic that does not slow down when the network is congested. It raises worries about fairness to other traffic, the quality users experience, and the danger of congestion collapse. It makes no recommendations about how to deploy voice over IP.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3714 explains why voice traffic on a congested network without delivery guarantees should respond to packet loss. It recommends that standards say when a flow that cannot slow down should stop or pause.

questions: why does voip need congestion control
when should a voip call stop sending
what are iab concerns about voice traffic
subtitle: Why best-effort voice traffic needs congestion control when it cannot reduce its sending rate.

tldr.problem: Best-effort voice traffic with a minimum sending rate may continue sending during persistent packet loss. The IAB discusses the resulting risks to network efficiency, voice quality and fairness to other traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares such a flow with TCP sending at the same rate on the wire and discusses when the voice flow should stop or suspend if it cannot reduce its rate further.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends that standards for best-effort flows with a minimum sending rate specify a drop rate that triggers suspension or termination. It is not a complete protocol specification.

today: RFC 3714 is an Informational statement of concern and recommendations. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it, and the document does not specify a complete protocol.

sections.title: The Concern and an Example
sections.content:
The IAB raises concerns about voice traffic carried as best-effort data without effective end-to-end congestion control. It does not recommend a deployment path for Voice over IP, claim that best-effort service will provide acceptable call quality, or discuss signaling.

The RFC describes a demonstration call that used more than half of a 128 kbps access link. Its point is that a flow continuing at a high rate through heavy packet loss can use scarce capacity while still providing poor service to its users.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Architecture Board asks what happens when voice traffic keeps sending on a busy link. Its example shows that one call can consume much of a shared link even while packets are being lost.

sections.title: Three Effects of Persistent Packet Loss
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three concerns. Congestion collapse can occur when packets use capacity on one congested link and are dropped farther along the path. High loss also harms call quality, and voice flows that do not reduce their rate can receive more bandwidth than congestion-controlled TCP flows experiencing the same loss.

The document's fairness comparison assumes a TCP flow with the same round-trip time and data packets of 1460 bytes. It rejects the idea that best-effort voice traffic should automatically be treated as more valuable than other best-effort traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Ongoing packet loss can waste capacity, make calls hard to understand, and leave less capacity for other Internet traffic. The network cannot know that one data flow is more valuable than another.

sections.title: Congestion-Control Work Discussed
sections.content:
The RFC reviews IETF work on RTP, TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC), the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP), and adaptive audio codecs. It notes that RTP guidance called for monitoring loss and comparing performance with TCP, while TFRC aimed to provide a smoother rate than TCP for some applications.

Adaptive codecs can reduce the amount of data sent when conditions worsen. The RFC distinguishes those approaches from fixed-rate voice flows that reach a minimum rate and cannot reduce it further.
sections.plainLanguage: Several methods discussed in the RFC can adjust to congestion, including protocols that control sending rates and audio encoders that use fewer bits. A fixed-rate flow needs another response once it reaches its minimum rate.

sections.title: When a Minimum-Rate Flow Should Stop
sections.content:
The RFC proposes comparing a voice flow's rate on the wire with the rate a TCP connection could maintain under the same conditions. If the voice flow cannot reduce its rate and sends significantly more than that TCP flow during persistent loss, it should terminate or suspend sending.

For the examples in the RFC, at a round-trip time of 0.1 seconds, a flow with a 4.75 kbps minimum rate should stop when persistent loss significantly exceeds 40%; a flow with a 64 kbps minimum should stop when it significantly exceeds 25%. The RFC leaves details such as the measurement interval and when a suspended flow resumes to future protocol work.
sections.plainLanguage: If a voice flow cannot send less, it should pause or stop when ongoing packet loss is too high compared with a data transfer under the same conditions. The RFC gives example thresholds, but does not define a complete procedure for measuring or resuming a flow.

sections.title: Recommendation and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that IETF standards for best-effort flows with a minimum sending rate specify a packet-drop rate above which the flow terminates or suspends. It says the chosen rate should be consistent with the analysis and tables in the document.

The RFC is guidance to the IETF community, not a finished protocol. It also says adaptive variable-bit-rate codecs are preferable for shared Internet use and notes that additional mechanisms would be needed before UDP applications could safely use Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN).
sections.plainLanguage: The recommendation is for standards writers to specify when a minimum-rate flow must pause or stop. The RFC does not itself define the protocol behavior that carries out that recommendation.
